title: Interview: Jordan Ellis (Senior Backend Engineer)

calendarEvent.title: Interview: Jordan Ellis (Senior Backend Engineer)
calendarEvent.description:
System design round: design a calendar-sync service that ingests Google and Microsoft webhooks reliably.

Interviewers: Shreyas (lead), Priya (reliability and security).
Candidate profile and scorecard are in Ashby. Please submit written feedback before any debrief.

Join with Google Meet: https://meet.google.com/qvr-hnzk-tpe

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Hey Jordan, can you hear me okay?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Hi, yes, I can hear you. Can you hear me?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Loud and clear. Priya should be joining in a second, she's just wrapping up another call.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: No problem at all.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Where are you calling in from?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Lisbon. It's six in the evening here and the sun's still out, so I really can't complain.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: That's a good evening. We've had rain all week, so I'm a little jealous.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Ha. I moved here from Dublin about four years ago, and the weather was, uh, a big part of the decision.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: I can imagine. Have you picked up much Portuguese?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Enough to order food and apologize. My neighbours are patient with me.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Hi, sorry, I'm here. Hi Jordan, I'm Priya.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Hi Priya, nice to meet you.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So, quick intros. I'm Shreyas, co-founder and CTO at Deino. Priya is our staff engineer for infrastructure and security.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Which mostly means I worry about things breaking and people breaking in.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Ha. Those are the two important ones.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Plan for the next forty-five minutes. About ten minutes on your background, then twenty-five or so on a system design problem, and then we leave time for your questions at the end. Sound good?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Sounds great, let's do it.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Cool. So tell us a bit about yourself and what you're working on right now.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Sure. I've been doing backend work for about eight years now. Right now I'm at a payments company, on the team that owns webhook ingestion.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: So we receive events from card processors, banks, a few wallet providers, and we verify them, normalize them, and fan them out to internal services.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Peak is somewhere around nine thousand events a second, around Black Friday. A normal day is a lot lower than that.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And before the payments company?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Before that I spent about three years at a CRM startup, where I built the sync engine. Two-way sync of contacts, email and calendar events with Gmail and Outlook.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: So, um, I have scars from both the Google and the Microsoft APIs.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: That's very relevant, as you'll see in about ten minutes.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: What languages have you been working in?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Mostly Go at the payments company, some Kotlin. At the CRM it was Python and then Go. I've written some Rust on side projects but nothing in production.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Our backend is Rust, so that's good to know. People pick it up, it just takes a few weeks.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: On the CRM sync engine, how did you handle conflicts? Someone edits an event in Outlook and in your app at the same time.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: We started with last-writer-wins on the whole event, and that was a mistake. People would lose a location change because someone else edited the title a second later.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: We moved to field-level merge. We kept the last version we'd synced as a base, diffed both sides against it, and only flagged a conflict when the same field changed on both sides.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And when the same field did change on both sides?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Provider won for time and attendees, our app won for our own custom fields. It wasn't elegant, but it was predictable, and support could explain it to customers.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: What's on-call like where you are now?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Weekly rotation, about one week in eight. It's busy because a lot of our partners have incidents, and we feel them. I'm used to it, but I'd like it to be a bit calmer.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: What's the hardest production incident you've been part of at the payments company?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Probably the one where a processor replayed about two days of events after their own outage. All at once, no warning.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Our dedupe table was keyed on their event ID, which saved us on correctness. But the replay saturated our queue and delayed live events by about forty minutes.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: What changed in the design afterwards?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: We split it into lanes. Live traffic and replay traffic go to different queues with different consumers, so a backfill can never starve the live path.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Who drove that change, you or someone else?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: I proposed it in the postmortem and built it with one other engineer. It took about three weeks, mostly because of the migration.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And why are you looking now?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Honestly, I want to be closer to the product. At the payments company I'm three layers away from anybody who uses what I build.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: And the sync work at the CRM is the work I've enjoyed most. So a company where calendar sync is core to the product is pretty appealing.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Okay, that's a great segue. Let's get into the design part. Give me a second to share my screen.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Can you see a doc with a heading that says calendar sync?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Yep, I can see it.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So here's the problem. Deino syncs technicians' calendars with Google and Microsoft 365. Today we poll every five minutes.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: We want to move to webhooks. Design a service that ingests Google and Microsoft webhooks reliably and keeps our copy of each calendar correct.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Okay. First, are we only doing Google and Microsoft? No CalDAV, no iCloud?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Just Google and Microsoft. Let's keep iCloud out of it.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: And what's the scale? How many calendars, and how fresh does it need to be?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: About forty-five hundred connected calendars today, and plan for fifty thousand. On freshness, we'd like a change to show up in Deino within thirty seconds most of the time.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Let me do some quick math on that, just to size things. Fifty thousand calendars, and on a busy morning maybe a third of them change within an hour.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: That's on the order of five to ten notifications a second on average, with spikes. So this isn't a throughput problem, it's a correctness problem.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: That's how we think about it too.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: And is the data flowing one way, provider into Deino, or two-way?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: It's two-way in the product, but for this exercise focus on the inbound side. We can talk about writes if there's time.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Okay. Let me start with what the providers actually send, because it shapes everything else.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Google push notifications don't carry the event data. You call events.watch on a calendar, you get a channel, and Google sends you a ping that basically says something changed on this resource.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Then you call events.list with your sync token to get the actual changes since last time.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Microsoft Graph is different. You create a subscription, and the notification tells you which resource changed. You can also get rich notifications with the data encrypted in the payload, but most people still go back and fetch, or use a delta query.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Right, that matches what we see today.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: So in both cases I'd treat the webhook as a hint, not as data. The source of truth is the provider's API with a cursor, which is the sync token on Google and the delta link on Microsoft.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: For the data model, I'd have a connections table per user and provider holding the encrypted credentials, a calendars table, a subscriptions table for channels and Graph subscriptions, and a sync state row per calendar with the current cursor.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Then the events themselves, keyed on the provider's identifiers. I'll come back to the key, because that's where the bugs live.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Before you go further, how do you know a webhook is really from Google?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Google doesn't sign the notifications the way, say, Stripe does with an HMAC header. What you get is a channel token that you set yourself when you create the watch.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: So I'd generate a random token per channel, store a hash of it, and compare it in constant time on every request.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Plus you check that the channel ID and the resource ID map to a channel you actually created and that's still active. Anything else gets a 4xx and increments a metric.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: And what about Microsoft, how do you verify those?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Microsoft has the clientState field. Same idea, a secret you set per subscription, and they echo it back in every notification.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: And when you create a subscription, Graph sends a validation request with a validationToken query parameter. You have to echo it back as plain text within ten seconds, or the subscription isn't created.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: If you turn on rich notifications, they also include validation tokens as JWTs that you can verify against Microsoft's signing keys. I'd verify those too.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: What about replay? Someone captures one valid request and sends it a thousand times.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Because the notification is only a hint, a replay is mostly harmless for correctness. It just triggers a fetch, and the fetch is idempotent.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: But it is a cost and a rate-limit problem. So I'd rate-limit per channel at the edge and coalesce: if there's already a pending sync for that calendar, another ping doesn't add more work.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Where does the webhook endpoint itself run? Same service as the rest of the API?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: I'd keep it as a separate small service behind its own ingress. It doesn't need access to tokens or the events database at all, only the channel lookup and permission to write to the queue.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: So if someone finds a bug in the parsing code, the blast radius is that they can enqueue junk, not read anyone's calendar.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Okay, that makes sense. Keep going.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: So, the ingestion path. My first instinct is to keep it really simple. The webhook handler validates the request, takes a lock for that calendar in Redis, calls Google or Graph to fetch the changes, writes them to our database, releases the lock, and returns 200.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: That gives you per-calendar ordering, because only one handler can hold the lock for a given calendar at a time.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Can I push on that a bit?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Yeah, please, go ahead.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Graph expects a response within about three seconds, or it treats the delivery as failed and retries. If you're holding the request open while you wait for a lock and then do a round trip to Google, one slow API call turns into a retry storm from Microsoft.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: And a Redis lock with a TTL isn't really a mutual exclusion guarantee. If the handler pauses longer than the TTL, two of them think they hold the lock and you've got two writers on the same calendar.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Yeah. That's fair, both of those. I think I conflated two things, validating the request and doing the work.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Let me redo it. The handler does only the cheap stuff: validate the token or clientState, look up the channel, write a small message to a queue, and return 202.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: No outbound calls in the request path at all. That should be comfortably under a hundred milliseconds, even at the ninety-ninth percentile.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Then for ordering, instead of locks, I'd partition the queue by calendar ID. Everything for one calendar is processed in order by one consumer at a time, so you don't need a distributed lock.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: And if the consumer dies halfway through?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Then the message becomes visible again and another consumer picks it up. That's at-least-once delivery, so processing has to be idempotent. Which I'll get to in a second.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: And actually, because Google's ping has no payload, the order of the pings barely matters. What matters is that syncs for one calendar are serialized, and that you only advance the sync token after you've committed the changes.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Say more about that last part.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: The worker reads the stored sync token, calls events.list, and writes the changed events and the new sync token in the same database transaction.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: If it crashes before commit, the old token is still there and you just fetch the same page again. If it commits, the next run starts from the new token. So the cursor and the data can never disagree.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: What if the worker commits, but crashes before it deletes the message from the queue?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Then the message comes back and gets processed again. But the sync token has already moved forward, so the fetch returns nothing new and the upserts are no-ops. That's the whole point of making the write path idempotent.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: And if the queue itself is down when the webhook arrives?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Then the handler can't enqueue, so it returns a 503 and lets the provider retry. Google retries with backoff on server errors, and Graph keeps retrying for a few hours.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: And if all of that fails, the reconciliation sweep picks it up later, which I'll get to. I'd never return 200 for something we didn't durably store.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: I like that you said same transaction. We've been bitten by exactly that.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: What would you actually use for the queue? Kafka, SQS, something else?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: At fifty thousand calendars, honestly, I wouldn't run Kafka for this. It's a lot of operational weight for a small team.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: I'd use SQS FIFO with the message group ID set to the calendar ID. You get ordering per group, and the content-based dedupe window helps with duplicate pings.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: FIFO queues used to have pretty tight throughput limits. Does that worry you?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: High-throughput mode mostly fixed that, and we're talking hundreds of messages a second at peak, not tens of thousands. If it ever became a problem, Kafka partitioned by calendar ID is the same design with more knobs.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Fair enough, I'd make the same call at our size.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Talk about idempotency more concretely. What's the key?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Two levels. At ingest, a dedupe key so the same notification doesn't create two queue messages. For Google that's the channel ID plus the X-Goog-Message-Number header.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: For Graph there's no per-notification ID, so I'd hash the subscription ID, change type, resource and timestamp, and keep that in a dedupe table with a TTL of a day or so.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: But the real idempotency is at write time. Every event is upserted by a natural key: provider, calendar ID, event ID, and for recurring events the recurrence instance, so the original start time of that occurrence.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: And you compare the etag, or the change key on Microsoft, so an older version of an event can never overwrite a newer one.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Why the recurrence instance specifically?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Because a recurring series where one occurrence was moved comes back as the master event plus an exception. If you key on just the event ID, or just the iCalUID, the exception and the master collide. Or worse, you create a second copy of the moved occurrence.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Yeah. Funny you say that.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Did I just describe a bug you've had?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: You may have. Let's keep going.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: What happens when a sync token goes bad?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Google returns a 410 Gone when the sync token is invalid or expired. Then you have to do a full sync: drop the token, list the calendar from scratch, and reconcile against what you have stored.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: For a technician calendar I'd bound the full sync to a time window, say thirty days back and six months forward, so you're not pulling ten years of someone's dentist appointments.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: And you reconcile by marking anything you didn't see as deleted, but only inside that window. Outside the window you don't touch anything.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: And during the full sync, more pings come in.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: They queue up behind it on the same message group, so they run afterwards. And because they're coalesced, ten pings during a full sync turn into one incremental sync once it's done.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: What about time zones? Technicians travel, and people do strange things with all-day events.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Store exactly what the provider gives you, the start with its time zone, plus a normalized UTC instant for scheduling. All-day events stay as dates, not midnight UTC, otherwise they shift a day for anyone west of Greenwich.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: And recurring events need the series time zone, because a weekly nine o'clock meeting stays at nine across a daylight saving change, and the UTC instant moves.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: How do deletes show up?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: On Google, an incremental sync returns deleted events with status cancelled, so you have to handle that explicitly rather than just upserting. On Graph, the delta query gives you an at-removed marker. Both of those need tests, because they're easy to get wrong silently.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Okay, renewals. How do you keep the subscriptions alive?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: It's different on each side. Google channels expire and you can't extend one. So you create a new channel before the old one expires, run both briefly, and then call channels.stop on the old one.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Duplicate pings during the overlap are fine because of the coalescing and the idempotent writes.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Graph subscriptions for Outlook events last a bit under three days at most, so you PATCH the expiration date before it lapses.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: I'd have a subscriptions table with an expires_at column, and a scheduler that renews anything past about half of its lifetime. That leaves plenty of room for retries if Graph is having a bad day.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Graph also sends lifecycle notifications. reauthorizationRequired, subscriptionRemoved, and missed. Missed is basically Microsoft telling you it dropped some notifications and you should resync.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: What's your alert if renewals silently stop working?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: A gauge of subscriptions that expire in the next twelve hours and haven't been renewed. That number should be zero. If it's above zero for more than one scheduler cycle, page someone.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Okay. Now say webhooks just don't arrive. Google has an incident, or our endpoint was down for twenty minutes.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Then you need a safety net, and that's a reconciliation sweep. Every calendar gets an incremental sync on a timer even if there was no ping, maybe every hour, with jitter so they don't all fire at once.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: An incremental sync with a valid token and no changes is cheap, it's one request. So it doesn't cost much quota, and it bounds how stale a calendar can get even if every single webhook is lost.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: And if our endpoint was down, I'd trigger a sweep for every calendar right after recovery, through a separate replay lane, not the live lane. Same lesson as the payments incident.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So basically you're keeping polling.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: I'm keeping slow polling as a backstop. Webhooks give you freshness, polling gives you correctness. I wouldn't rely on webhooks alone with any provider.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Let's talk rate limits. Fifty thousand calendars, and everybody edits their calendar at eight on Monday morning.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Google has per-project and per-user quotas, and you get a 403 with rateLimitExceeded or a 429. Graph returns 429 with a Retry-After header.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: For Graph you honor Retry-After exactly. For Google, exponential backoff with full jitter, capped at a minute or two.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: But the more important thing is fairness. I'd put a token bucket per tenant in front of the fetch workers, so one big customer onboarding three hundred technicians doesn't starve everyone else.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Where does a message go when it's failed too many times?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Dead-letter queue after, say, eight attempts, with an alert and a tool to redrive. But for sync I'd treat a dead-lettered calendar as needing a full sync, rather than something a human has to read through.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: One more on security. You're holding OAuth refresh tokens for fifty thousand people's calendars. Where do they live?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Not in the same table as everything else, and not in plaintext. Envelope encryption with a KMS key, in a separate table, and only the sync workers' role can decrypt.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Request the narrowest scope you can, calendar events rather than broad account access. And log every decrypt, so you can see if something unusual is reading tokens.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: And when a refresh token gets revoked?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: You mark the connection as broken and surface it in the product, so the dispatcher knows that technician's calendar isn't syncing. Retrying a revoked token forever just burns quota and hides the problem.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: You mentioned writes earlier. Quick one: when Deino writes a job into a technician's Google calendar, that write triggers a webhook back to us. How do you avoid loops?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Tag the events you create, with extended properties on Google or an open extension on Graph, and store the etag you got back from your own write.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: When the sync sees an event whose etag matches what you just wrote, you skip it. Without that you get echo loops, or at least a lot of wasted work.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Okay, last area. How do you know the whole thing is working? What's on the dashboard?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: The number I'd care about most is freshness: for each calendar, the time since its last successful sync. And an end-to-end latency metric, from when the notification hits our endpoint to when the change is committed.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Then the boring ones: queue depth and the age of the oldest message, the 410 rate, error rates by provider, dead-letter queue size, and that subscriptions-expiring gauge.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: And I really like a canary. A couple of test calendars on each provider, and a job that creates and moves an event every few minutes, including a moved occurrence of a recurring event, and measures how long until it shows up correctly in Deino.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Including the recurring case.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Especially the recurring case, apparently.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: And tracing, across the queue?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: A correlation ID minted at ingest, carried in the queue message and into the worker logs and the database write. So for any change to a calendar you can answer which ping caused it.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: How would you roll this out? We have forty-five hundred calendars on polling today, and customers notice when sync breaks.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Run both in parallel first. Webhooks on, polling still on, and compare what each one would have written, per calendar, without the webhook path actually writing.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Once the diff rate is basically zero for a couple of weeks, flip a per-tenant flag so the webhook path writes, and slow polling down to the hourly sweep. Start with internal calendars and one friendly customer.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And testing, before any of that?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Recorded provider responses for the weird cases, the recurring exceptions, cancelled events, the 410. And a fake provider in the test suite that can drop or duplicate notifications on purpose, so you can prove the sweep catches what the webhooks miss.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Okay, we're at about the thirty-five minute mark, so let's stop there and switch to your questions. What would you like to know?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: A few things. First, team size. How big is engineering, and who would I work with day to day?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: We're fourteen people in total. Engineering is seven, including me and our support engineer.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: This role would sit with Maya, she's the tech lead on Calendar Sync v2, which is, well, pretty much what we just designed.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Ha. Okay, that's what I was hoping you'd say.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Second, on-call. What does it look like in practice?

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Weekly rotation, with a primary and a secondary. With the current team you'd be primary about one week in six. We use PagerDuty.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Most weeks are quiet. I won't pretend every week is.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: We had a rough September, honestly. A sync bug duplicated jobs for some customers, and the person on call carried a lot of it. Spreading that load better is part of why we're hiring.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: I appreciate you being upfront about it. Is there any comp time after a bad on-call week?

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Yes. If you get paged overnight, you take the next morning off. It's informal, but people actually do it.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Good. And third, remote, since I'm in Lisbon and I want to stay in Lisbon.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: How does that work for you, and how many people are remote today?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: We're remote-friendly. We have an office and some people come in, but about half the team is fully remote.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: What we ask for is at least four hours of overlap with the core team's working day.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: That works for me. I'm looking for remote with real time zone overlap, not a fully async role. I'm fine working until seven or eight in the evening Lisbon time a few days a week.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: That's roughly what our other remote folks do.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Okay. And what would success look like for this role in the first ninety days?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Honestly, being a real second pair of hands on Calendar Sync v2. Beta is planned for mid-November and GA in early December, so you'd likely be landing right in the middle of it.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Shipping something real to production in your first month is normal here. We don't do long onboarding programs.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Okay. Those were my big ones. Oh, and is there a budget for conferences, that kind of thing?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: There is, it's modest, but people use it. We can share the details later in the process.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: A couple of logistics from our side before we let you go. What's your notice period?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: It's four weeks, that's what's in my current contract.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And do you have a range in mind for compensation?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: I'm looking at a hundred and fifteen to a hundred and thirty thousand euros base. I'm open on the mix of equity and base, depending on the overall package.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Okay, that's helpful. We'll be transparent about our bands if we move to the next step.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: On next steps, Priya and I will each write up feedback, and we'll get back to you by Wednesday, October seventh, either way.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Great. Is there anything you'd like from me in the meantime? References, anything like that?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Not yet. If it moves forward, we'd ask for references at that point.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Usually the next stage is a conversation with Aisha, our CEO, and a pairing session with Maya on some real code. But we'll confirm all of that when we get back to you.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Sounds good. Pairing on real code sounds more fun than another whiteboard.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And I'll send you the doc we have on how on-call and remote work at Deino, so you have it in writing. I'll send it over tonight.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: That would be great. Thank you both, this was genuinely a fun conversation.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Thanks Jordan. Enjoy the rest of the sunshine.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Will do. Bye, have a good weekend.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Okay, he's gone. Let's not debrief yet.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Agreed. Write first, talk later, otherwise we just anchor on each other.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Can we both get written feedback into Ashby by end of day today?

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Yes, I'll have mine in Ashby by end of day today.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Same, I'll have mine in by end of day too, right after my next call. Then we compare once both are in.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: I might ask Maya if she wants to do a follow-up round with him. But she's pretty wiped after September, so maybe not.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Let's see. Also, we floated adding a take-home for this role. I'm leaning against it, the design round covers the same ground.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Agree, no take-home. It mostly filters out people with kids and a current job.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Okay, no take-home. Talk later.
